R-privacy-1 (Account deletion keeps the member's email, name, phone and postal address) is high and still open; fix it, or a human accepts the risk or defers it

findings.evidence: "UPDATE users SET deleted_at = datetime('now'), password_hash = NULL WHERE id = ?",
findings.recommendation: The proposal promises that the button "erases the member's personal data", yet delete_account only sets deleted_at and clears password_hash: after a member deletes their account, the users row still holds email, display_name, phone and postal_address (app/schema.sql:3-6) indefinitely, with no purge. A member exercising their right to erasure (GDPR Art. 17) keeps all their contact data in the users table, and the orders kept for accounting still point at it through orders.user_id, so they are not "without personal data" either. Overwrite or null the personal columns in the same UPDATE (e.g. email replaced by a non-identifying tombstone such as 'deleted-<id>' to satisfy NOT NULL UNIQUE, display_name by a placeholder, phone and postal_address set to NULL), and add a test asserting those columns no longer hold the member's data. State how long backups keep the erased data before it expires.
findings.title: Account deletion keeps the member's email, name, phone and postal address

findings.recommendation: The change adds a per-member analytics identifier that nothing in the change calls and that the proposal does not mention, and delete_account does nothing about analytics events already keyed by it: with a fixed salt the id stays linkable to the member after deletion. Either drop it from this change, or state its purpose and processor and make account deletion reach the analytics data. Confidence is low because the callers and the analytics pipeline are not visible in this diff.
findings.title: New analytics identifier added with no use and outside the erasure
